Nowicki et al. (2022) compared POCO graphites with grain sizes of 1 µm (AF-5) and 10 µm (S-180) and found that coarser-grained graphite yields higher material removal rate (MRR) but also greater relative tool wear, whereas the finer-grained AF-5 produced the lowest surface roughness (Ra). (Nowicki et al. 2022) The later work by the same group extends these observations for EDM with negative polarity and reports that fine-grained graphite increases process efficiency while reducing tool wear; the authors link detached graphite grains to instability in discharge behaviour and altered removal mechanisms, and they provide mathematical models to predict MRR, relative tool wear rate (TWR) and Ra from machining parameters. (Nowicki et al. 2024)

Across the reviewed EDM studies, pulse energy metrics (principally discharge current (peak current) and pulse duration) emerge repeatedly as the dominant factors controlling both MRR and surface roughness. Nowicki et al. identify discharge current and pulse duration as the main drivers of MRR and Ra for both graphite grades, and they find the time interval (pulse off-time) most influential for relative graphite electrode wear. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Complementary experimental designs using Taguchi methods show peak current to be the single most influential factor on MRR and Ra in cryogenically treated superalloy workpieces, with ANOVA attributing 86.43% and 74.79% influence of peak current on MRR and Ra respectively in that study. (Ramabalan et al. 2024) Broad reviews and surveys of EDM process enhancements report a range of auxiliary approaches (cryogenic treatment, powder-mixed dielectrics, ultrasonic assistance, and others) that aim to reduce TWR and improve MRR and surface integrity. (Shastri et al. 2022) Studies on nanopowder-mixed dielectrics coupled with electrode cryogenic treatment indicate substantial reductions in electrode wear and overcut for brass electrodes in other materials, demonstrating the potential of combined process modifications to improve dimensional accuracy and EWR. (Sana et al. 2024)

Electrical discharge coating (EDC) and related surface-modification techniques are also discussed in the literature as routes to modify surface properties via discharge processes, but information connecting these coating approaches directly to electrode selection for Hastelloy EDM is not provided in the available sources. Nowicki et al. (2022) tested two POCO graphites (AF-5, 1 µm grain; S-180, 10 µm grain) and found that coarser-grained graphite yields higher material removal rates but incurs greater relative tool wear, while the fine-grained AF-5 produced the smoothest surfaces; discharge current and pulse duration were the principal drivers of MRR and Ra, and the time interval dominated relative tool wear for both grades (Nowicki et al. 2022). A later study by the same group extends this comparison for negative polarity EDM and reports that using fine-grained graphite improves process efficiency and reduces tool wear; the authors also observe that detached graphite grains influence discharge stability and removal mechanics, and they derive mathematical models to predict MRR, relative TWR and Ra from process settings and electrode grain size (Nowicki et al. 2024).

Experiments using design-of-experiment techniques show peak current (amperage) and pulse-on time strongly govern both MRR and TWR outcomes; Taguchi/ANOVA analyses attribute the largest fraction of variance in MRR and Ra to peak current in at least one alloy study, and general EDM work reports amperage as the dominant factor for MRR, TWR and surface integrity metrics (Nas & Kara 2022)(Akıncıoğlu 2022). Complementary work on Hastelloy B2 links high current and long pulse duration to accelerated electrode-edge degradation: square electrodes become rounded at the ends as a result of unstable sparking and heat diffusion, making electrode taper, radius and wear length highly sensitive to those thermal parameters (Ramabalan et al. 2024).

To mitigate high tool wear and unstable removal, the literature discusses multiple auxiliary techniques. Reviews and experimental reports list cryogenic treatment, powder-mixed dielectrics, ultrasonic assistance and other hybrid methods as ways to improve MRR, reduce TWR and refine surface integrity; one systematic review surveys these approaches and highlights remaining gaps for process optimization (Shastri et al. 2022). Nanopowder-mixed EDM studies and trials with cryogenically treated electrodes demonstrate large reductions in electrode wear and overcut for specific material–electrode combinations, though these results come from aluminium/brass systems and rely on complex experimental optimisation and predictive models such as ANN–MOGA linked to RSM datasets (Sana et al. 2024).

Surface modification during EDM is also exploited: electrical discharge coating (EDC) techniques can produce protective or functional layers on workpieces, which is relevant when surface integrity or coating formation is a goal alongside material removal (Liew et al. 2020).

Studies that compare graphite electrodes with different grain sizes report consistent effects on MRR, TWR and surface roughness. Nowicki et al. 2024 extended this comparison for negative polarity EDM and concluded fine-grained graphite raised process efficiency while reducing tool wear, and that detached graphite grains influence discharge stability and removal efficiency (Nowicki et al. 2024).

Nowicki et al. 2022 report discharge current and pulse duration as the main determinants of MRR and Ra for both AF-5 and S-180 graphite, while the inter-pulse time dominates relative tool wear of graphite (Nowicki et al. 2022). Nowicki et al. 2024 modelled the combined effects of electrode grain size and machining settings on MRR, relative TWR and Ra, producing mathematical relations intended to predict outcomes for parameter selection (Nowicki et al. 2024). Experiments on Titanium (Gr2) using Taguchi and ANOVA likewise identified amperage as the dominant factor for MRR and TWR in that alloy’s EDM trials (Akıncıoğlu 2022).

Nanopowder-mixed EDM combined with neural-network-based optimisation has demonstrated large reductions in electrode wear and overcut for brass electrodes under specific dielectrics and treatments, illustrating how dielectric additives and electrode conditioning alter wear behaviour (Sana et al. 2024). For square-hole machining of Hastelloy B2, current and pulse duration strongly affect electrode wear and edge rounding, with thermal diffusion transforming sharp electrode geometry into hemispherical end shapes under unstable sparking conditions (Ramabalan et al. 2024).

Additively manufactured 18Ni-300 (maraging) steels produced by selective laser melting (SLM) exhibit distinctly fine, rapidly solidified microstructures in the as-built condition, with ultrafine submicron grains and martensitic matrix that reflect very high cooling rates during layerwise melting and solidification. (Tan et al. 2018) SLM parts often reach near-full density when parameters are optimised, which permits production of functional components with limited porosity. (Yap et al. 2015) The SLM process therefore imposes an intrinsic thermal history that both refines grains and promotes in situ tempering and precipitation phenomena not typically present in conventionally manufactured counterparts. (Haghdadi et al. 2020)

Electron microscopy studies report abundant nanoscale needle-shaped precipitates (Ni3X, X = Ti, Al, Mo) dispersed within the martensitic matrix after standard SLM fabrication, and these precipitates are linked to the material’s age-hardening response. (Tan et al. 2018) In one detailed microstructural survey, the as-fabricated microstructure is described as fine-grained martensite with no strong crystallographic texture across build orientations, and an as-printed surface roughness around $Ra\approx 10\ \mu$m prior to any surface finishing. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) The hierarchical (sub)grain structures and fine precipitates induced by AM correlate with enhanced strength and wear resistance relative to conventional materials in several reviews. (Haghdadi et al. 2020)

Thermal treatments alter these SLM microstructures by promoting precipitate evolution, stress relief and, under particular intercritical regimes, partial reversion of martensite to austenite. (Tan et al. 2018) Studies that apply solution treatment, aging or combinations including plasma nitriding at temperatures near typical aging cycles document microstructural dependence of the thermochemical layer morphology and of mechanical and corrosion-related properties. (Godec et al. 2021) Optimised aging produces maximum nano-hardness and is associated with precipitation-controlled hardness; aging also shifts corrosion potentials in heat-treated material. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) Plasma nitriding performed without prior aging can produce defects in the compound layer, whereas nitriding applied after prior heat treatments improves wear and corrosion resistance of SLM maraging steel. (Godec et al. 2021)

Reversed (reverted) austenite formed by tempering in the intercritical $\alpha' + \gamma$ range has a clear effect on localized corrosion performance in chloride media. (Khan et al. 2022) An intercritical temper at $720^\circ\mathrm{C}$ produced reversed austenite at martensite lath boundaries, driven by local Ni enrichment from intermetallic dissolution, and the specimens with this reversed austenite showed higher pitting potential, lower corrosion current density and reduced corrosion rate in $3.5\ \mathrm{wt}\%$ NaCl compared with as-printed, aged, or homogenised samples lacking reverted austenite. (Khan et al. 2022) General corrosion and tribological testing across as-built and heat-treated SLM maraging steels have been characterised and compared to wrought counterparts, indicating that despite finer microstructure, corrosion behaviour in heat-treated conditions can be similar to conventional material and that precipitation phenomena play a central role in both hardness and corrosion response. (Tan et al. 2018)(Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

###

Selective laser melting (SLM) uses a high-power laser to melt and fuse metal powder layer by layer, producing near-net-shape parts with up to 99.9% relative density under appropriate parameters (Yap et al. 2015). The layerwise, high-energy input of SLM drives a unique microstructural evolution in steels, creating hierarchical (sub)grains and fine precipitates that differ from conventionally produced counterparts (Haghdadi et al. 2020).

Multiple studies report a very fine martensitic microstructure in as-built 18Ni-300 maraging steel produced by SLM, consistent with extremely high cooling rates; one study measured submicron grain size with an average of $0.31\ \mu$m and inferred cooling rates on the order of $10^{7}\ \mathrm{K/s}$ (Tan et al. 2018). Electron microscopy in SLM maraging steel reveals dense distributions of needle-shaped nanoprecipitates of Ni$_3$X (X = Ti, Al, Mo) within the martensitic matrix, which contribute to age hardening by mechanisms discussed as Orowan bowing and coherency strain hardening (Tan et al. 2018). A separate microstructural survey found that as-printed SLM maraging steel is a fine-grained martensitic structure that shows no preferred texture between the XY, XZ and YZ sections and has a surface roughness around $R_a\approx 10\ \mu$m (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021).

Heat treatments applied to SLM maraging steel alter precipitate morphology, relieve residual stress and can reduce mechanical anisotropy; systematic comparisons of as-fabricated and heat-treated specimens show that aging increases hardness while reducing residual stress (Tan et al. 2018). Studies that combine thermochemical treatments with prior solution or aging steps report that the sequence of heat treatments affects surface compound layers produced during nitriding: nitriding without prior aging produced cracks in the compound layer, whereas nitriding after suitable heat treatment improved wear and corrosion resistance of the additive-manufactured material relative to untreated nitrided samples (Godec et al. 2021).

Reversion of martensite to austenite through intercritical heat treatment alters local chemistry and morphology and influences corrosion in chloride media: tempering within the $\alpha' + \gamma$ range at $720\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ produced reversed austenite concentrated along martensite lath boundaries, driven by local Ni enrichment from dissolution of intermetallics, and this specimen exhibited a higher pitting potential and lower corrosion current density in 3.5 wt% NaCl than as-printed, aged, or homogenized samples (Khan et al. 2022). That study frames reversed austenite as improving pitting resistance of SLM maraging steel in chloride solution, while also noting that the broader impact of martensite-to-austenite reversion on corrosion properties remains insufficiently understood in the literature (Khan et al. 2022).

Surface condition also affects corrosion outcomes: electropolishing reduced SLM surface roughness by about 65% and, together with precipitation state after heat treatment, was associated with comparable nano-hardness and corrosion behaviour between heat-treated SLM and wrought maraging steel (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021). Reviews of AM steels emphasize that the distinctive AM microstructures often enhance strength, wear and corrosion resistance compared with conventional routes, but achieving acceptable ductility and fatigue performance is still a challenge and limits application-driven assessments of corrosion under service conditions (Haghdadi et al. 2020)(Afkhami et al. 2019).

Household adoption of rooftop photovoltaic (PV) systems is constrained by a combination of financial, informational, technical and institutional barriers identified across the literature. Financial constraints (both the magnitude of upfront cost and concerns about long‑term returns) figure prominently: empirical analyses indicate that government subsidies reduce perceived investment risk and act as a primary incentive for households contemplating PV, while lower equipment prices and reduced maintenance costs further strengthen the investment case. (Parsad et al. 2020)

Affordability and payment flexibility recur as decisive determinants of uptake in lower‑income contexts. National survey evidence from Uganda shows that affordability explains variation in the type of solar product adopted and that flexible payment mechanisms increase the likelihood that income‑constrained households acquire more expensive solar home systems. (Aarakit et al. 2021) Similar findings from Pakistan identify system cost as a negative predictor of willingness to adopt, alongside perceived risk, indicating that monetary barriers combine with risk perceptions to suppress demand. (Tanveer et al. 2021)

Beyond direct cost, policy design and institutional implementation shape household choices. Reviews of India’s national solar targets and policy instruments describe ambitious capacity goals and the centrality of rooftop PV in meeting them, and they discuss policy instruments intended to accelerate rooftop deployment while highlighting implementation challenges. (Goel 2016) Case‑level investigation of a smart‑grid pilot in Puducherry used household surveys to probe space availability, consumer experience and responses to government initiatives, revealing practical impediments even within policy pilot projects. (Kappagantu et al. 2015)

Non‑financial inhibitors (especially limited technical knowledge and awareness) also matter. Multimethod research in India finds that knowledge and awareness variables, together with technical barriers, significantly influence household investment decisions and help forecast adoption outcomes; these non‑financial factors ranked highly when models combined structural equation results with artificial neural network forecasts. (Tanveer et al. 2021)

Policy interventions appear centrally relevant to household investment decisions. A structural modelling study using Kerala household surveys finds that government subsidies function as a primary motivator by reducing the initial investment risk for households, and that both low prices and low maintenance costs further encourage investment; the authors conclude that subsidies and financial factors are among the strongest motivators for PV adoption (Parsad et al. 2020). Local pilot surveys in Indian projects gather consumer experience data specifically to probe user familiarity and technical readiness for rooftop systems (Kappagantu et al. 2015).

Institutional and policy barriers
Reviews of the Indian renewable sector catalogue institutional and systemic constraints that impede deployment despite strong solar resources and national targets; such reviews also present recommendations for policy and stakeholder actions to overcome obstacles facing the sector (J & Majid 2020).
